Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "the lantern film society at merrow college is planning a screening of the last orchard, a 1986 film, for friday october 18. the meeting to sort the event was on october 2 in student union room 3, and eleven active members were there. the screening is listed for arts 214, with the film starting at 7:15 p.m. and the doors opening at 6:45. the room has 72 seats, which is why the group chose it instead of the smaller seminar room, though the film society has not worked out how many people might come. the event is part of the society's regular fall program and is not being described as a festival or a special campus-wide event.

at the meeting, president leah park kept the discussion on practical jobs rather than on whether members liked the film. she said, “If the room feels too bright, people may miss the first few minutes while they settle in.” that was a concern about the lighting and not a request to delay the start. joel, who is coordinating the room, has asked the campus facilities desk whether the side lights can be dimmed, but he has not heard back yet. the main overhead lights need to stay available while the audience enters, so the society is considering using only the front half of the room if the side lights cannot be adjusted. nobody has made that choice yet.

1. room and access. arts 214 has a level entrance from the east corridor, but the corridor door is sometimes locked after 6:30. members will check the building's evening access notice and put the correct entry point on the society's printed flyer. this is a check of campus information, not a request for a new door arrangement. the room has movable chairs, and the group expects to set out 60 of them, leaving space near the back for people who arrive with mobility devices. members are to count the chairs again before the event because the room is also used for a class earlier that day. no one has checked yet whether the class will leave the chairs in rows or in a circle.

2. projection and sound. the society's projector is in a locked cabinet in the media lab, and priya has the key. she will inspect the projector and the two HDMI cables that the club already owns during her lab shift on october 10. she is not being asked to borrow or buy equipment. the film file is on a college drive, and the copy listed there is 4.6 gigabytes. sam has watched the opening minute on a laptop, but he has not tested the file through the room's projector or speakers. the society has a small portable speaker, though it may not be loud enough for the room. the film has subtitles in english, and the group plans to check that the subtitle track appears on the projection before doors open.

money and outside services came up briefly because the treasurer's sheet lists $180 as remaining in the term activity account. she has not checked whether that figure is still current or whether any of it can be used for this screening. in the meeting notes, leah wrote: do not contact vendors. for this planning stage, the restriction means no calls, emails, messages, or visits to vendors about the screening, including questions about prices, equipment, printing, food, or transport. it applies to vendors, not to college staff or society members. the members may check the equipment already owned by the college and review the society's own stored receipts, but they are not to use those checks as a reason to approach a vendor. the group has not received a newer instruction about this restriction.

the society will use its existing email list and the notice board by the library for publicity. nora has drafted a short announcement with the title, date, start time, door time, room number, and the film's running time of 94 minutes. she has not posted it because joel still needs to confirm the accessible entrance information from the evening access notice. the society does not have a confirmed poster design yet. members may make a simple text-only version in the meantime, but nobody has been assigned to print it, and no printing order has been made. the announcement will say that the screening is free; this was already written in the society's program sheet for the term.

some details of the evening are still divided between people, and there is no single event checklist yet. priya is handling the projection check, joel is checking room access and lighting, and nora is working on the announcement. the treasurer is keeping the account figure in her notes until she can verify it. two newer members, cal and ren, offered to arrive early and help arrange chairs, but they have not been given a time because the society has not settled who will unlock the room. they can still check the room inventory during normal building hours, which does not require a special entry arrangement. leah asked that any changes to the screening time be shared with the whole group before they appear on a flyer.

members also discussed how to handle questions from people who have not attended a society screening before. the library notice board is visible from the main walkway, but the email list reaches only students who signed up at an earlier event. nora suggested adding a line that says viewers can ask a member at the door about the subtitle display or the seating area. the group has not decided whether a member should stand near the east corridor entrance, since that depends on the access notice and the person who will have the key. no names have been added to a door-duty list. the society's old folding sign is stored in the media lab, but its lettering is worn, so members may inspect it before deciding if it can be used.

an unrelated item from the same meeting was the society's small archive of screening notes. cal found a folder from the previous spring with handwritten comments on four films, and ren offered to scan the pages for the society's shared drive. the folder is kept in a labeled drawer in the student union office, not in the media lab with the projector. they have not started scanning it, and the pages include member names, so ren plans to ask the group how those names should be handled before uploading anything. this archive task is separate from the october screening and does not change the event arrangements.", "output": "The Lantern Film Society at Merrow College is planning a screening of the 1986 film *The Last Orchard* for Friday, October 18. Eleven active members attended the planning meeting on October 2 in Student Union Room 3. The screening is listed for Arts 214, with the film starting at 7:15 p.m. and doors opening at 6:45 p.m. The room has 72 seats, which is why the group chose it over the smaller seminar room, although the society has not estimated how many people may attend. The event is part of the society’s regular fall program, not a festival or a special campus-wide event.

At the meeting, president Leah Park kept the discussion focused on practical tasks rather than on whether members liked the film. She said, “If the room feels too bright, people may miss the first few minutes while they settle in.” This was a concern about the lighting, not a request to delay the start. Joel, who is coordinating the room, has asked the campus facilities desk whether the side lights can be dimmed, but he has not received a reply. The main overhead lights need to remain available while the audience enters. If the side lights cannot be adjusted, the society is considering using only the front half of the room. No decision has been made.

1. Room and access. Arts 214 has a level entrance from the east corridor, but the corridor door is sometimes locked after 6:30 p.m. Members will check the building’s evening access notice and put the correct entry point on the society’s printed flyer. This involves checking campus information, not requesting a new door arrangement. The room has movable chairs, and the group expects to set out 60, leaving space near the back for people who arrive with mobility devices. Members will count the chairs again before the event because the room is also used for a class earlier that day. No one has yet checked whether the class will leave the chairs in rows or in a circle.

2. Projection and sound. The society’s projector is in a locked cabinet in the media lab, and Priya has the key. During her lab shift on October 10, she will inspect the projector and the two HDMI cables the club already owns. She is not being asked to borrow or buy equipment. The film file is on a college drive, and the copy listed there is 4.6 gigabytes. Sam has watched the opening minute on a laptop, but he has not tested the file with the room’s projector or speakers. The society also has a small portable speaker, although it may not be loud enough for the room. The film has English subtitles, and the group plans to check that the subtitle track appears on the projection before the doors open.

Money and outside services came up briefly because the treasurer’s sheet lists $180 as remaining in the term activity account. She has not checked whether that figure is current or whether any of the money can be used for this screening. In the meeting notes, Leah wrote: do not contact vendors. At this planning stage, the restriction means no calls, emails, messages, or visits to vendors about the screening, including questions about prices, equipment, printing, food, or transport. It applies to vendors, not to college staff or society members. Members may check equipment already owned by the college and review the society’s stored receipts, but they must not use those checks as a reason to approach a vendor. The group has received no newer instruction about the restriction.

The society will use its existing email list and the notice board by the library for publicity. Nora has drafted a short announcement with the film title, date, start time, door time, room number, and 94-minute running time. She has not posted it because Joel still needs to confirm the accessible entrance information from the evening access notice. The society does not yet have a confirmed poster design. Members may make a simple text-only version in the meantime, but no one has been assigned to print it, and no printing order has been placed. The announcement will say that the screening is free, as already stated in the society’s program sheet for the term.

The evening’s details are still divided among several people, and there is no single event checklist. Priya is handling the projection check, Joel is checking room access and lighting, and Nora is working on the announcement. The treasurer is keeping the account figure in her notes until she can verify it. Two newer members, Cal and Ren, offered to arrive early and help arrange chairs, but they have not been given a time because the society has not settled who will unlock the room. They can still check the room inventory during normal building hours, which does not require a special entry arrangement. Leah asked that any changes to the screening time be shared with the whole group before they appear on a flyer.

Members also discussed how to respond to questions from people who have not attended a society screening before. The library notice board is visible from the main walkway, but the email list reaches only students who signed up at an earlier event. Nora suggested adding a line saying viewers can ask a member at the door about the subtitle display or seating area. The group has not decided whether a member should stand near the east corridor entrance, since that depends on the access notice and the person who will have the key. No names have been added to a door-duty list. The society’s old folding sign is stored in the media lab, but its lettering is worn, so members may inspect it before deciding whether it can be used.

Another item from the same meeting was the society’s small archive of screening notes. Cal found a folder from the previous spring with handwritten comments on four films, and Ren offered to scan the pages for the society’s shared drive. The folder is in a labeled drawer in the Student Union office, not in the media lab with the projector. They have not started scanning it, and the pages include member names. Ren plans to ask the group how those names should be handled before uploading anything. This archive task is separate from the October screening and does not change the event arrangements."}]
